verses.zh: 主耶和华又指示我一件事：我看见一筐夏天的果子。
verses.en: The Sovereign Lord showed me this: I saw[NOTE:1] a basket of summer fruit.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “behold” or “look.”
The basket of summer fruit (also in the following verse) probably refers to figs from the summer crop, which ripens in August-September. See O. Borowski, Agriculture in Iron Age Israel, 115.
verses.commentary:
8:1 "Thus the Lord God showed me, and behold" This phrase was used to
introduce the first three visions in chapter 7. Because of its recurrent use it shows that the visions are related
(cf. Amos 7:1,4,7; 8:1).

▣ "a basket of summer fruit" There is a word play in the Hebrew text between the word for "fruit" (קיצ, BDB 884, KB 1098)
and the word for "end" (קצ, BDB 893, KB 1118, cf. Dan. 8:17,19; 11:40; 12:4,6) in Amos 8:2. These two words would have been
pronounced the same way (cf. NIDOTTE, vol. 3, p. 920).

Summer fruit (BDB 884) is the last fruit of the season, which over ripens very quickly in the heat and
was appropriate imagery for the spiritual rottenness of the Israeli nation. They were over-ripe for judgment!

verses.zh: 他说：「阿摩司啊，你看见甚么？」我说：「看见一筐夏天的果子。」耶和华说：「我民以色列的结局到了，我必不再宽恕他们。」
verses.en: He said, “What do you see, Amos?” I replied, “A basket of summer fruit.” Then the Lord said to me, “The end[NOTE:1] has come for my people Israel! I will no longer overlook their sins.[NOTE:2]
notes: There is a sound play here. The Hebrew word קֵץ (qets, “end”) sounds like קָיִץ (qayits, “summer fruit”). Possibly they were pronounced alike in the Northern dialect of Hebrew. This is a case where the vision is not the prophecy, but simply the occasion for a prophecy. The basket of summer fruit is only relevant as a means to get Amos to say qayits (קָיִץ) as an occasion for the Lord to say qets (קֵץ) and make the prophecy. Cf. Jer 1:11-14; Amos 7:7-8.
Heb “I will no longer pass over him.”
verses.commentary:
8:2 "‘The end has come for My people Israel'" The VERB (BDB 97, KB 112, Qal
PERFECT) denotes that the covenant between YHWH and Abraham's descendants will be abrogated
with the northern tribes.

The pain of YHWH can be sensed in the covenant phrase, "My people Israel"( cf. Hosea 11:1-4,8), but
it will not be completely abrogated. There is hope (cf. Amos 9:7-15; Hosea 11:9-11).

To allow the appearance of the covenant to continue would be cruel. YHWH's judgment, as
painful as it was, was an act of love with a real potential of restoration (cf. Amos 9:14-15)!

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT PROMISES TO THE PATRIARCHS

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

SPECIAL TOPIC: EASTERN LITERATURE (biblical paradoxes)

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

▣ "will spare them no longer" This phrase is very emphatic. Literally, it is "I will never (BDB 414, KB 418,
Hiphil IMPERFECT) again pass by them" (BDB 716, KB 778, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT).

The Covenant is broken (cf. Amos 7:8)! His people have rejected Him by their amalgamation with
Canaanite fertility worship for the last time. In Gen. 15:16 the Amorites of the Promised Land were rejected because of
their godless lifestyle. Now YHWH's own people are being turned out because of their similar godless lifestyle. God's
patience coming to an end. This is clearly seen in Isa. 6:9-13; Jer. 15:5-9 and Ezek. 7:2-9.

verses.zh: 主耶和华说：「那日，殿中的诗歌变为哀号；必有许多尸首在各处抛弃，无人作声。」
verses.en: The women singing in the temple[NOTE:1] will wail in that day.” The Sovereign Lord is speaking. “There will be many corpses littered everywhere![NOTE:2] Be quiet!”
notes: Or “palace” (NASB, NCV, TEV).

Heb “Many corpses in every place he will throw out.” The subject of the verb is probably impersonal, though many emend the active (Hiphil) form to a passive (Hophal): “Many corpses in every place will be thrown out.”
verses.commentary:
8:3

NASB
"the songs of the palace"

NKJV, NRSV, Peshitta
"the songs of the temple"

REB, NJB
"the palace songs"

TEV
"the songs in the palace"

JPSOA
"the singing women of the palace"

LXX
"the ceilings of the temple shall howl"

The term "songs" (BDB 1010) is FEMININE PLURAL, which may
denote the irony that the female singers (same Hebrew root revocalized) at court would become the professional
mourners. But, there were so many bodies that the only sound was silence! (For a brief discussion of mourning rites see Roland deVaux, Ancient Israel,
vol. 1, pp. 56-61.)

There is a possibility of two translations:

- "palace" (TEV, NJB, cf. Amos 6:5)

- "shrine" or "temple" (cf. Amos 5:23)

Because of Amos 8:10 (cf. Amos 5:23) option #2 seems best.

SPECIAL TOPIC: GRIEVING RITES

▣ "will turn to wailing" The VERB (BDB 410, KB 413, Hiphil PERFECT with waw)
occurs several times in the section of Jeremiah dealing with judgment on the surrounding nations (cf. Jer. 47:2; 48:20,31,39;
49:3; 51:8). He seems to follow Isaiah's usage (cf. Isa. 13:6; 14:31; 15:2,3; 16:7[twice]; 23:1,6,14). A good translation of this
outcry over death and destruction could be "wail," "howl," "shriek."

The eighth century minor prophets used this imagery several times in relation to YHWH's coming judgment.

- Hosea 7:14

- Joel 1:5,11,13 (date unknown, possibly early post-exilic)

- Amos 8:3

- Micah 1:8

▣ "in that day" This was a standardized imagery for judgment used so often in the eighth
century prophets. YHWH will visit His people for

- blessing (cf. Amos 9:11,13)

- cursing (cf. Amos 1:14; 2:16; 3:14; 4:2; 5:8,18,20; 6:3; 8:3,9,10,11,13)

- See full note at Amos 2:16.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THAT DAY

▣ "they will cast them forth in silence" This refers to abnormal burial practices (i.e. no professional wailing
nor any wailing at all) because of invasion and siege. This phrase is related to Amos 6:10 (the same INTERJECTION
is used, BDB 245, "hush").

SPECIAL TOPIC: BURIAL PRACTICES

verses.zh: 你们这些要吞吃穷乏人、使困苦人衰败的，当听我的话！
verses.en: Listen to this, you who trample[NOTE:1] the needyand do away with[NOTE:2] the destitute in the land.
notes: See the note on the word “trample” in 2:7.
Or “put an end to”; or “exterminate.”
verses.commentary:
8:4 "Hear" This is the Hebrew term Shema (BDB 1033, KB 1570, Qal IMPERATIVE).
It means "to hear so as to do." It is often used of prayer (cf. Deut. 6:4-6; Amos 3:1,13; 4:1; 5:1).

SPECIAL TOPIC: LISTEN/HEAR (shema)

▣ Verse 4 refers to subjugation (i.e. "trample" or "crush" BDB 983, KB 1375, Qal PARTICIPLE)
of the poor ("the needy" parallel to "the humble of the land" and "the helpless. . .the needy," cf. Amos 8:6) by the
rich and politically powerful (cf. Amos 2:7; 5:11,12).

The JPSOA suggests an emendation to the MT of this verse, which reads, "who on every new moon
devour the needy, and on every sabbath the humbled of the land" (i.e. vv. 4-5).

verses.zh: 你们说：月朔几时过去，我们好卖粮；安息日几时过去，我们好摆开麦子；卖出用小升斗，收银用大戥子，用诡诈的天平欺哄人，
verses.en: You say, “When will the new moon festival[NOTE:1] be over,[NOTE:2] so we can sell grain? When will the Sabbath end,[NOTE:3] so we can open up the grain bins?[NOTE:4] We’re eager[NOTE:5] to sell less for a higher price,[NOTE:6] and to cheat the buyer with rigged scales![NOTE:7]
notes: Apparently work was prohibited during the new moon festival, just as it was on the Sabbath.
Heb “pass by.”
The verb, though omitted in the Hebrew text, is supplied in the translation from the parallel line.
Heb “sell grain.” Here “grain” could stand by metonymy for the bins where it was stored.
Here and in v. 6 the words “we’re eager” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

Heb “to make small the ephah and to make great the shekel.” The “ephah” was a unit of dry measure used to determine the quantity purchased, while the “shekel” was a standard weight used to determine the purchase price. By using a smaller than standard ephah and a heavier than standard shekel, these merchants were able to increase their profit (“sell less for a higher price”) by cheating the buyer.

Rigged scales may refer to bending the crossbar or shifting the center point of the scales to make the amount weighed appear heavier than it actually was, thus cheating the buyer.tn Heb “and to cheat with deceptive scales”; cf. NASB, NIV “dishonest scales,” NRSV “false balances.”
verses.commentary:
8:5 The wealthy, powerful, and influential could not wait for the religious assemblies (i.e. "new moon,"
cf. Num. 28:11; 2 Kgs. 4:23 and "sabbath," cf. Exod. 31:13-17) to be over so they could instigate their illegal, improper,
and unjust schemes toward the poor:

- to make the bushel smaller

- the shekel bigger

- use dishonest scales

- sell the husk of the wheat (those grain heads that fell in the dirt, BDB 655, or under-developed grain that fell
through the sieve, cf. Amos 9:9) with the wheat

All of these refer to cheating the poor when they buy food (cf. Lev. 19:35-36; Deut. 25:13-16; Prov. 20:10).

The VERBS "sell" (BDB 991, KB 1404) and "open" (BDB 834, KB 986) are both
COHORTATIVE. These merchants' desire to exploit is so strong that their actions are the commands
of their own hearts.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FEASTS OF ISRAEL, II

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANE WEIGHTS AND VOLUMES (metrology)

▣ "the new moon" This refers to the ancient custom of observing a religious holiday at the first of the
month (cf. Num. 28:11; 2 Kgs. 4:23). Remember, the Jews went by the lunar calendar.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FEASTS OF ISRAEL, II. D.

▣ "dishonest scales" This CONSTRUCT (BDB 24, 941) denotes unfair and dishonest
commercial enterprises, especially against the poor (cf. Micah 6:10-11). YHWH hates this falsehood (cf. Prov. 11:1). It is
never "business is business" with God or His people! Exploitation reveals a heart of self, greed, and fallenness.

verses.zh: 好用银子买贫寒人，用一双鞋换穷乏人，将坏了的麦子卖给人。
verses.en: We’re eager to trade silver for the poor,[NOTE:1] a pair of sandals[NOTE:2] for the needy.We want to mix in some chaff with the grain!”[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “to buy the poor for silver.”sn The expression trade silver for the poor refers to the slave trade.
See the note on the word “sandals” in 2:6.
Heb “The chaff of the grain we will sell.”
verses.commentary:
8:6 This verse gives an example of how poor people who could not buy food were forced to sell themselves
or their family members into slavery (i.e. the rich Israeli family for a period of time; this does not refer to the Phoenician slave trade)
for a small amount (i.e. "a pair of sandals," cf. Amos 2:6).

These wealthy merchants sank so low as to sell grain mixed with husk, dirt, pebbles, etc. With
profits from these fraudulent sales they purchased more slaves! Therefore, the poor paid for the exploitation of the poor!

verses.zh: 耶和华指着雅各的荣耀起誓说：他们的一切行为，我必永远不忘。
verses.en: The Lord confirms this oath[NOTE:1] by the arrogance of Jacob:[NOTE:2] “I swear[NOTE:3] I will never forget all you have done![NOTE:4]
notes: Or “swears.”

In an oath one appeals to something permanent to emphasize one’s commitment to the promise. Here the Lord sarcastically swears by the arrogance of Jacob, which he earlier had condemned (6:8), something just as enduring as the Lord’s own life (see 6:8) or unchanging character (see 4:2). Other suggestions include that the Lord is swearing by the land, his most valuable possession (cf. Isa 4:2; Ps 47:4 [47:5 HT]); that this is a divine epithet analogous to “the Glory of Israel” (1 Sam 15:29); or that an ellipsis should be understood here, in which case the meaning is the same as that of 6:8 (“The Lord has sworn [by himself] against the arrogance of Jacob”).
The words “I swear” are not in the Hebrew text but have been supplied in the translation because a self-imprecation is assumed in oaths of this type.
Or “I will never forget all your deeds.”
verses.commentary:
8:7 "The Lord has sworn by the pride of Jacob" In Amos YHWH swears several
times as a way to show that His words are true:

- "The Lord God has sworn by His holiness," Amos 4:2

- "The Lord God has sworn by Himself," Amos 6:8

- "The Lord has sworn by the pride of Jacob," Amos 8:7

This phrase has several possibilities:

- God's glory in the descendants of Jacob (cf. 1 Sam. 15:29). The TEV translates this as "The
Lord, the God of Israel, has sworn"

- since no where else does God swear by another person, this may mean, "the Lord,
of whom Israel is so proud, has sworn" (UBS, Handbook, p. 165)

- that the people of Jacob had become so permanently wicked that YHWH could swear by their settled condition (cf. Amos 6:8)

▣ "I will never forget any of their deeds" This is a very strong and emphatic statement.

- a HYPOTHETICAL PARTICLE, (אט)

- a Qal IMPERFECT VERB, "to forget" (BDB 1013, KB 1489)

- the NOUN "everlasting," "perpetuity" (BDB 664)

These exploitative merchants will answer for the crimes against both their covenant brothers
and sisters and their covenant God!

verses.zh: 地岂不因这事震动？其上的居民不也悲哀吗？地必全然像尼罗河涨起，如同埃及河涌上落下。
verses.en: Because of this the earth[NOTE:1] will quake,[NOTE:2] and all who live in it will mourn.The whole earth[NOTE:3] will rise like the Nile River;[NOTE:4] it will surge upward[NOTE:5] and then grow calm,[NOTE:6] like the Nile in Egypt.[NOTE:7]
notes: Or “land” (also later in this verse).
It is not clear whether the speaker in this verse is the Lord or the prophet.
Heb “all of it.”

The movement of the quaking earth is here compared to the annual flooding and receding of the Nile River.tc The MT reads “like the light” (כָאֹר, khaʾor; note this term also appears in v. 9), which is commonly understood to be an error for “like the Nile” (כִּיאוֹר, kiʾor). See the parallel line and Amos 9:5. The word “River” is supplied in the translation for clarity. If this emendation is correct, in the Hebrew of Amos “Nile” is actually spelled three slightly different ways.
Or “churn.”
Or “sink back down.” The translation assumes the verb שָׁקַע (shaqaʿ), following the Qere.

The entire verse is phrased in a series of rhetorical questions that anticipate the answer, “Of course!” (For example, the first line reads, “Because of this will the earth not quake?”). The rhetorical questions entrap the listener in the logic of the judgment of God (cf. 3:3-6; 9:7). The rhetorical questions have been converted to affirmative statements in the translation for clarity.
verses.commentary:
8:8 This question expects a "yes" answer (the land has a regular expected pattern). This verse is apparently using the imagery of

- an earthquake mentioned in Amos 1:1

- the destruction caused by the annual flooding of the Nile River in Egypt (cf. Amos 9:5; Jer. 46:7-8)

Because this VERB (BDB 176, KB 204, Niphal PERFECT with
waw) is used to describe Jonah being driven from the presence of YHWH (cf. Jonah 2:4), it may be imagery
for exile from the Promised Land (cf. Amos 9:1-4,5). This same word was used of YHWH driving the Canaanites out
of the Promised Land, but now Israel is being removed for her sins and idolatry (cf. Gen. 15:12-21)!

▣

NASB
"the land quake"

NKJV, NJB, Peshitta
"the land not tremble"

NRSV
"the land tremble"

REB
"the earth quake"

TEV
"the earth will quake"

LXX
"the land be troubled"

The MT has the VERB (BDB 919, KB 1182, Qal IMERFECT)
"quake." The term "land" (BDB 75) can refer to Palestine or the whole region (see SPECIAL TOPIC: LAND, COUNTRY, EARTH).
The PRONOUN "it" in vv. 8b,c,d; 10e,f, refers back to "land."

Apparently Amos is using both the major earthquake and the annual floodiing of the Nile (i.e. flood imagery of
destruction) as parallel, denoting Israel's judgment. This imagery may go back to the Song of Moses in Exod. 15, esp. v. 14 (also
note 1 Sam. 14:15).

SPECIAL TOPIC: WATERS/SEA

▣

NASB, NRSV, TEV, NJB, REB, JPSOA
"the Nile"

NKJV
"the River"

LXX, Targums, Vulgate
"a river"

Peshitta
"a flooded river"

The MT has two forms.

- כאר ‒ like the light (line c, see imagery in v. 9)

- כיאור ‒ like the Nile (line e, cf. Amos 9:5)

The UBS Text Project, p. 293, suggests that both spellings refer to the Nile River. However,
it gives "the Nile" a "C" rating (considerable doubt). "The light" (i.e. option #1) does not make sense in
this verse, but it might in v. 9.

verses.zh: 主耶和华说：到那日，我必使日头在午间落下，使地在白昼黑暗。
verses.en: In that day,” says the Sovereign Lord, “I will make the sun set at noonand make the earth dark in the middle of the day.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “in a day of light.”
verses.commentary:
8:9 This verse has been understood in several ways:

- eschatological language (i.e. "in that day") like Amos 5:18-20; Isa. 13:10; Joel 2:2; 3:15; Micah 3:6

- a reference to the plagues on Egypt, which form the basis of the curses of Deuteronomy 27-29

- a literal reference to an eclipse (cf. Amos 5:18-20)

In a sense the cosmic chaos of creation is recurring. The ideal setting of YHWH fellowshipping
with mankind has again been disrupted. Nature is seen as being in chaos (cf. Rom. 8:19-22).

It is ironic that water can be for destruction (i.e. flood) or a symbol of God's blessing
(cf. Amos 5:24). Mankind will experience one or the other! For an interesting discussion of the word "sea"
see NIDOTTE, vol. 2, pp. 461-466.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THAT DAY

SPECIAL TOPIC: WATERS

▣ "make the earth dark in broad daylight" This VERB (BDB 364, KB 361, Hiphil
PERFECT with waw) refers to YHWH's action. It may reflect the plague of darkness in Egypt (cf. Exod. 10:21-22;
Ps. 105:28). Here it refers to God bringing darkness, both literal (cf. Amos 5:8) and figurative (cf. Amos 8:11-12). Israel's
light is darkened (cf. Jer. 13:16).

SPECIAL TOPIC: DARKNESS

SPECIAL TOPIC: LIGHT

verses.zh: 我必使你们的节期变为悲哀，歌曲变为哀歌。众人腰束麻布，头上光秃，使这场悲哀如丧独生子，至终如痛苦的日子一样。
verses.en: I will turn your festivals into funerals[NOTE:1] and all your songs into funeral dirges.I will make everyone wear funeral clothes[NOTE:2] and cause every head to be shaved bald.[NOTE:3] I will make you mourn as if you had lost your only son;[NOTE:4] when it ends it will indeed have been a bitter day.[NOTE:5]
notes: Heb “mourning.”
Heb “I will place sackcloth on all waists.”sn Mourners wore sackcloth (funeral clothes) as an outward expression of grief.

Shaving the head or tearing out one’s hair was a ritual act of mourning. See Lev 21:5; Deut 14:1; Isa 3:24; 15:2; Jer 47:5; 48:37; Ezek 7:18; 27:31; Mic 1:16.tn Heb “and make every head bald.” This could be understood in a variety of ways, while the ritual act of mourning typically involved shaving the head (although occasionally the hair could be torn out as a sign of mourning).
Heb “I will make it like the mourning for an only son.”
Heb “and its end will be like a bitter day.” The Hebrew preposition כְּ (kaf) sometimes carries the force of “in every respect,” indicating identity rather than mere comparison.
verses.commentary:
8:10 This is a series of mourning rites (i.e. funeral songs, sackcloth, baldness) over YHWH's judgments of
Israel's worship times. Their worship will be turned to bitter mourning, like the death of an only son (cf. Jer. 6:26; Zech. 12: 10).

SPECIAL TOPIC: GRIEVING RITES

▣ "baldness" Because of Israel's connection with the Canaanite fertility cults, this could refer to
"shaving" (cf. Moab, Isa. 15:2; Jer. 48:37; Philistia, Jer. 47:5; and Phoenicia, Ezek. 27:31), which had cultic connotations (cf. Lev. 21:5).

But it could also refer to the pulling out of the hair of the head as a sign of mourning (cf. Micah 1:16; Ezek. 7:18).

SPECIAL TOPIC: GRIEVING RITES

▣ "a bitter day" This word (BDB 600) is used at the grief over a death (cf. Amos 5:16-17). They were
expecting just the opposite (cf. Amos 5:18-20)! This is a veiled reference to "that day," "the day of the
Lord." See note at Amos 2:16.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THAT DAY

verses.zh: 主耶和华说：日子将到，我必命饥荒降在地上。人饥饿非因无饼，干渴非因无水，乃因不听耶和华的话。
verses.en: Be certain of this,[NOTE:1] the time is[NOTE:2] coming,” says the Sovereign Lord, “when I will send a famine through the land—not a shortage of food or waterbut an end to divine revelation.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “behold” or “look.”
Heb “the days are.”
Heb “not a hunger for food or a thirst for water, but for hearing the words of the Lord.”
verses.commentary:
8:11 This may be the OT origin of one part of Jesus' beatitudes (cf. Matt. 5:6) and possibly a reference
to Matt. 4:4, where Jesus quotes Deut. 8:3. Israel thought she had all she needed, but what all of us really need
is fellowship with God (i.e. based on the revelation of His word)! Oh, what a terrible famine (cf. v. 12d; 1 Sam. 3:1;
2 Chr. 15:3; Ps. 74:9; Lam. 2:9; Ezek. 7:26)!

verses.zh: 他们必飘流，从这海到那海，从北边到东边，往来奔跑，寻求耶和华的话，却寻不着。
verses.en: People[NOTE:1] will stagger from sea to sea,[NOTE:2] and from the north around to the east. They will wander about looking for a message from the Lord, but they will not find any.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “they”; the referent (people) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
That is, from the Mediterranean Sea in the west to the Dead Sea in the east—namely, across the whole land.
It is not clear whether the speaker in this verse is the Lord or the prophet.
verses.commentary:
8:12 This shows a frantic but futile search for God. What shocking imagery! God has been seeking
mankind in love, but there will come a day when they will not be able to find Him. Humans were created to need
fellowship with God (cf. Gen. 1:26-27). Hell is the removal of the possibility of being with Him!

SPECIAL TOPIC: Seek the Lord

▣ "from sea to sea" For a speaker in Palestine, this would refer to the Mediterranean to the Dead
Sea. It is not very far physically, but it signifies from one end of the country to the other.

verses.zh: 当那日，美貌的处女和少年的男子必因干渴发昏。
verses.en: In that day your[NOTE:1] beautiful young women[NOTE:2] and your[NOTE:3] young men will faint from thirst.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “the.”
Or “virgins.”
Heb “the.”
It is not clear whether the speaker in this verse is the Lord or the prophet.
verses.commentary:
8:13 Even the young and strong will not be able to find God. Exhausted young people are imagery
for YHWH's judgment (cf. Isa. 51:20).

verses.zh: 那指着撒马利亚牛犊（原文是罪）起誓的说：但哪，我们指着你那里的活神起誓；又说：我们指着别是巴的神道（神：原文是活）起誓。这些人都必仆倒，永不再起来。
verses.en: These are the ones who now take oaths[NOTE:1] in the name of the sinful idol goddess[NOTE:2] of Samaria. They vow,[NOTE:3] ‘As surely as your god[NOTE:4] lives, O Dan,’ or, ‘As surely as your beloved one[NOTE:5] lives, O Beer Sheba!’ But they will fall down and not get up again.”
notes: Heb “those who swear.”

Heb “the sin [or “guilt”] of Samaria.” This could be a derogatory reference to an idol-goddess popular in the northern kingdom, perhaps Asherah (cf. 2 Chr 24:18, where this worship is labeled “their guilt”), or to the golden calf at the national sanctuary in Bethel (Hos 8:6; 10:8). Some English versions (e.g., NEB, NRSV, CEV) repoint the word and read “Ashimah,” the name of a goddess worshiped in Hamath in Syria (see 2 Kgs 17:30).
Heb “say.”

Your god is not identified. It may refer to another patron deity who was not the God of Israel, a local manifestation of the Lord that was worshiped by the people there, or, more specifically, the golden calf image erected in Dan by Jeroboam I (see 1 Kgs 12:28-30).

The MT reads, “As surely as the way [to] Beer Sheba lives,” or “As surely as the way lives, O Beer Sheba.” Perhaps the term דֶּרֶךְ (derekh, “the way”) refers to the pilgrimage route to Beersheba (see S. M. Paul, Amos [Hermeneia], 272), or it may be a title for a god. The notion of pilgrimage appears elsewhere in the book (cf. 4:4-5; 5:4-5; 8:12). The translation above assumes an emendation to דֹּדְךָ (dodekha, “your beloved” or “relative”; the term also is used in 6:10) and understands this as referring either to the Lord (since other kinship terms are used of him, such as “Father”) or to another deity that was particularly popular in Beer Sheba. Besides the commentaries, see S. M. Olyan, “The Oaths of Amos 8:14” Priesthood and Cult in Ancient Israel, 121-49.

This (BDB 79, KB 96) refers to

- the golden calves (cf. 1 Kgs. 12:28; Hosea 8:5-6; 10:5) set up at the cities of Dan and Bethel by Jeroboam I
(922 B.C.). They were meant to rival the temple in Jerusalem as a worship site for YHWH. All of
the kings of the northern tribes are condemned by the prophets because of these shrines.

- There is another possible understanding of this text based on the consonental Masoretic Text. It has the phrase, "the
Ashima of Samaria" (cf. 2 Kgs. 17:30). If so, this then would refer to the female fertility goddess of Canaan or
Syria (see NKJV, NJB footnotes, cf. 2 Kgs. 17:30).

Whichever reference is correct, it reflects the improper worship of the Northern Ten Tribes, Israel.

▣ "As the way of Beersheba lives" This is an unusual reference. Beersheba is a city located in
southern Judah. It was referred to earlier in Amos 5:5. Possibly the journey itself or the route with its cultic
associations or the term "way" is idiomatic of a ritual or teaching. Exactly how or what is involved in this idolatry
is uncertain.

It is just possible that a geographical emphasis is what is referred to (i.e. Dan to Beersheba,
cf. Jdg. 20:1; 1 Sam. 3:20), which would parallel Amos 8:12. These covenant people committed idolatry throughout
the Promised Land, but now they will frantically seek for YHWH again throughout the land, but will not find Him!

There is another option:

NASB, NKJV, NRSV, JPSOA
"the way"

"the god"

"the pilgrimage"

"the sacred way"

LXX
"your god lives"

Peshitta
"the cult"

NET
"your beloved one"

The MT has "the way" (BDB 202). There seems to be a parallel between

- "As your god lives, Dan"

- "As your _______ lives, Beersheba"

The NET Bible, p. 1602, suggests that "the way" may refer to

- a pilgrimage route, cf. Amos 4:4-5; 5:4-5; 8:12

- a title for a local god ("your beloved," an emendation, cf. Amos 6:10)

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible.
Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing
is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.
